quote: Vielleicht stellt sich auch heraus: es hat kei- nen Sinn zu sagen, es gäbe unlösbare Probleme.
english: Perhaps it will also turn out that it makes no sense to say there are unsolvable problems.
topic: Notes on freeing logic and epistemology from anthropomorphic thinking, on problems whose meta-question is best settled by solving them (twin primes, digits of pi), on a philosophical theory of experimentation and meaning applied to relativity and unsolvable problems, and on the axiomatic method in physics.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a precise mathematical conjecture. It is a philosophical or metamathematical remark: Hilbert suggests that the claim 'there are unsolvable (mathematical) problems' may have no meaning at all. In modern terms it touches two things: (a) relative undecidability, meaning statements that a given consistent, recursively axiomatized theory can neither prove nor refute, and algorithmic problems that no Turing machine can solve; and (b) absolute undecidability, meaning propositions that no humanly justifiable means of proof could ever settle. Gödel's disjunction is the modern framing of (b): either the mathematical mind cannot be mechanized, or there are absolutely undecidable problems. The note expresses Hilbert's 'non ignorabimus' stance, his 'axiom of solvability'.
triage.answered_by: There is no single answer. Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) and the negative solutions to the Entscheidungsproblem by Church and Turing (1936) showed that 'unsolvable problem' has a precise, meaningful sense relative to a formal system or to algorithms, and that such problems exist. This is commonly read as refuting Hilbert's conviction in its formal sense. Gödel's 1951 Gibbs lecture (the Gödel disjunction) reframed the absolute version. Whether absolutely undecidable propositions exist, or whether the notion even makes sense, is still debated in philosophy of mathematics, for example in Horsten & Welch (eds.), Gödel's Disjunction, OUP 2016.

evidence.claim: Hilbert said in his 1900 lecture that there is 'no ignorabimus' in mathematics. He often used the phrase to express his conviction that every mathematical problem can be solved. Church's and Turing's 1936 work settled the Entscheidungsproblem negatively.

A historical article on Hilbert's 'axiom of solvability' says this conviction is commonly regarded as falsified by Gödel's proof and by the negative results for the decision problem. The article argues the matter is subtler.
In 1951 Gödel set out a disjunctive thesis: either the mathematical mind is equivalent to a Turing machine, or there are absolutely undecidable problems. This is the subject of a 2016 OUP volume.
Recent work (Philosophia Mathematica) builds arguments about whether absolutely undecidable arithmetical propositions exist.

triage.why: The remark is a philosophical speculation about whether the concept of an 'unsolvable problem' is meaningful. It is not a well-posed mathematical statement, so it cannot be 'solved' as such. Later logic made relative unsolvability precise and showed it exists (Gödel 1931; Church and Turing 1936), which goes against Hilbert's hope in the formal sense. The absolute version, framed by Gödel's disjunction, is still an active philosophical research topic. The note is closely tied to Hilbert's published 'no ignorabimus' stance (1900 Paris address, 1930 Königsberg). It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. 'Active today' refers to that philosophical debate, not to mathematical research.
